author: William Saville

title: Tea, Salt and Smoke
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
Iroh arrived at Tideglass Cove carrying three teacups, a brass timer, and enough patience to make me suspicious.

Maui was beside the new sea-glass orchard trying to light a cooking fire with wood he had collected from the beach. The first piece was damp. The second was salt-soaked. The third produced a smell like someone had set a wet boot on fire.

"Why won't it catch?" he demanded.

"Because you're trying to burn the sea," I said.

"Very poetic. Not useful."

Iroh watched from the path.

"Would you like some dry kindling?" he asked.

Maui straightened.

"I can make fire! I've made fire in rain, on rocks, in front of crowds who were extremely grateful. These sticks are simply refusing to appreciate my résumé."

"I have no doubt. The question is whether you wish to make smoke first."

Maui regarded the dark plume rising from his little heap of wood.

"Perhaps I do not."

Iroh set down the cups. He had come to discuss planting herbs along the sheltered wall, but Fen had asked him to wait until the runoff from the new beds was tested. The salt level had dropped, though not enough for every cutting he wanted to grow.

We had an hour before the measurement.

Iroh opened a tin.

"Tea?"

Maui eyed it.

"Is it strong?"

"Strong enough for conversation."

"Then we'll need a bigger pot."

I sat beside the cold fire. Maui reluctantly followed. Iroh handed him the brass timer, a small device with a dial and a faint ticking sound.

"What is this?"

"A reminder that leaves require time in water."

Maui turned the timer over.

"I could make the water hotter."

"Then you might burn the leaves."

"I could make the leaves tougher."

"I recommend asking them first."

I laughed.

Maui looked between us.

"Are you two doing this on purpose?"

"Very little in life is entirely unplanned," Iroh said.

He poured the water and set the timer.

While we waited, Fen came down the path with the garden's salinity report. The sheltered bed was suitable for rosemary and sea kale, but the lower edge remained too brackish for the mint Iroh had hoped to plant.

"We'll keep the mint at Jasmine Steps," he said easily.

Maui looked impressed.

"You're not angry?"

"Why should I be?"

"You carried it all the way here."

"The plant will be happier elsewhere."

Fen sorted two jars of soil back into their carrying case. One smelled of wet stone; the other had a clean dry edge where salt had not reached the roots.

"Would either of you like to help label these?" Fen asked.

Maui straightened. "Naturally. Heroic handwriting is one of my greatest talents."

Iroh held out his pen. "Then the labels should be your undertaking."

Maui took the pen and stared at the numbers. They were small enough to be annoying and specific enough that a flamboyant signature would make them useless.

"One jar gets a number," Fen said. "Not a poem."

"You're denying the world literature."

"Yes. On this occasion."

Iroh chuckled into his tea. He had accepted the evidence and let go of the mint without treating it as a personal defeat. Maui was visibly struggling with the idea that being helpful could mean writing a two-digit sample code in an ordinary hand.

When he was done, Fen checked the numbers, sealed the lids and carried the case away. The planting committee could decide what belonged in the beds. Iroh would still have tea to brew at Jasmine Steps. Maui would still have to live in a world where every jar was not an opportunity for a legend.

I looked at him. He looked back, warning me with one eyebrow not to say the obvious thing.

I looked at Maui.

He looked at me.

"Don't say it," he warned.

"I wasn't going to."

"You were thinking something about the orchard."

"I contain many thoughts."

Iroh's eyes crinkled.

"Then you have plenty of material for an evening."

The timer rang.

Maui nearly dropped it.

"What kind of villain builds a bell that small?" Maui demanded, glaring at Iroh's timer.

"The kind who expects tea to steep for four minutes," Iroh answered.

"Four minutes? I've held the sun still longer than that."

"You must have been terribly bored."

Mini Maui lay flat on his stomach across the tattoos, pantomiming sleep. Maui gave his own chest an offended look. Iroh was laughing into his cup when the distant memory of the lower coastal bell made us all fall quiet.

Maui rolled the timer between his palms, suddenly gentle with it. His instinct was to run toward any sound that might mean danger. The idea of a locked passage waiting beneath the water plainly irritated him.

"All right," he said, working his grin back into place. "No heroic demolition today. But if that old bell decides to challenge me personally, I'm accepting."

Iroh lifted his cup. "Perhaps first we should discover whether it is a bell."

"You're both terrible for my reputation."

He drank the tea anyway. I could see that listening without doing anything spectacular was costing him more than he wanted us to know.

"That's a very small bell."

"Yes," Iroh said.

The word changed the air.

We had all heard the second bell beneath the cove several days earlier. It was still being measured. Fen had closed the lowest route while Danse and Tamsin examined the old structure. Neri had admitted the passage was sealed during the Closed Bells, though they still resisted naming everyone responsible.

Maui looked toward the water.

"Could the old bell be like this?"

"Perhaps," Iroh said. "But a bell is only a bell until we know who placed it and why."

"That sounds less exciting than a sea spirit."

"It is also easier to inspect."

I picked up my cup.

The tea tasted of toasted grain and citrus, the affordable house blend Iroh had developed after the poor mountain harvest. It wasn't the rare mint, and it didn't need to pretend it was.

"Good," I said.

Iroh smiled.

Maui sipped, considered, and said, "I could drink six cups."

"You may have one more."

"Why only one?"

"Because you are already remarkably energetic."

Maui laughed.

Fen came back from the drainage channel with mud on their sleeve and a request for two more buckets of clean water. The rosemary cuttings had been placed in the right bed, but the path to it was still slick.

Maui started to leap toward the shed. Iroh lifted one hand.

"Perhaps we should ask where the buckets are wanted before we carry them."

Fen looked from one to the other. "By the north path, not beside the stove. And don't pour them on the seedlings until I check the soil."

Maui stopped. "A man could lose his whole heroic reputation carrying water incorrectly."

"An alarming risk," Iroh said.

I laughed and went to fetch the buckets with him. The two men watched one another with a sort of guarded curiosity. Maui clearly wanted to impress Iroh, who had survived battles and chosen to run a tea shop. Iroh seemed amused by Maui's inability to let a quiet moment remain quiet.

Later, while the fire pit cooled, Iroh asked if I intended to stay at Tideglass that evening.

"I do," I said. "I have time for tea with you tomorrow if you'd like, but I don't want either of you assuming I can be in two places at once."

Maui picked up his cup. "That seems a shame. I'd be magnificent at sharing a schedule with two Jaspers."

"One of me is more than enough."

Iroh chuckled. "You have been very clear about preferring polyamory and ethical non-monogamy. An invitation is not diminished because it has to be accepted."

Maui looked down at his own hands. "I know that. Sometimes I'm still figuring out how to say I wish I had more time."

"Then say exactly that," I told him.

He met my eyes. "I wish I had more time."

The simple answer made my throat tighten. I squeezed his hand beneath the table, and Iroh politely became interested in rescuing a cup from the breeze.

When we rose to help clean the cooking area, neither man needed to prove himself better at warmth, wisdom or carrying stones. The tea had gone cold. The company hadn't.

The afternoon stretched out with ordinary work. We moved the dry rosemary cutting to the proper bed. I helped Fen check the drainage channel. Maui carried a crate of stones and, to his credit, did not turn the job into a challenge.

By evening the wind had shifted toward the shore. Iroh stayed to help us light a small cooking fire using properly dried wood and an ash pit set away from the growing beds. He explained the difference between a fire that warms people and one built to impress them.

"Do you ever want to impress someone?" Maui asked.

Iroh looked at me.

"Frequently. Usually I make a terrible fool of myself."

I felt my cheeks warm.

Maui grinned.

"So do I."

I stared at both of them.

"I have no idea why I spend time with either of you."

"Excellent judgment," Iroh said.

"Terrible taste," Maui added.

They laughed like men who had agreed not to compete for the evening. That mattered more to me than a perfect speech about how modern our relationships were.

After supper, Iroh returned to Jasmine Steps. He had work in the morning and wanted time to prepare it. We walked him to the upper path.

"Thank you for the tea," I said.

"Thank you for the company."

He touched my hand, warm and gentle, and waited until I returned the gesture. Maui stood a respectful distance away, checking the lanterns along the path.

"I'll see you at the pantry tomorrow," I said.

"I look forward to it."

Iroh bowed his head to Maui.

"Be gentle with your fire."

"Only if it behaves."

They smiled at each other.

When Iroh had gone, Maui fell into step beside me.

"He's good at waiting," he said.

"Yes."

"I'm trying."

"I know."

He was quiet for a while. The smoke from the cooking fire lingered faintly in our clothes. We passed the garden, where the sea kale stood in neat rows and the dry-slope herbs tilted toward the last light.

"Can I say something foolish?" he asked.

"Always."

"Sometimes I wonder how you can love more than one person and still know which way to walk home."

I stopped.

"Do you mean tonight?"

He nodded.

I took his hand.

"I don't love Iroh because you're missing something. I don't love you because anyone else is missing something. I care about different people for different reasons, and I've chosen to be honest about that. Tonight I want to come home with you."

He studied my face.

"And tomorrow?"

"Tomorrow I have tea with Iroh. And then I'll decide how to spend the rest of the day. The agreement isn't that everybody gets the same hours. It's that we tell each other what we can actually offer."

Maui breathed out.

"That makes sense."

"Does it feel okay?"

"Mostly."

"Mostly is a good beginning."

He smiled, a little shy.

"I want to be the person you can tell when mostly isn't enough."

"You already are."

I stepped closer. He leaned down to meet me, and the kiss was warm and slow, tasting faintly of citrus tea. For once neither of us had a clever remark ready.

We walked home after the lanterns were lit.

The little brass timer stayed with Iroh. The second bell remained a mystery beneath the tide.

I was learning that patience could be an act, not just the absence of movement.
